rows.claim: All rightful judgment and power in this world operate through God's judgment and power; in the Hereafter God judges directly among His creatures, to whom they return.
rows.anchor: In this world, all judgment and power are rightfully exercised only as a function of God’s Judgment and Power,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse was reportedly revealed to advise Muslims to emigrate from Makkah to Abyssinia, where they could practice their religion freely.
rows.anchor: This verse was reportedly revealed to advise some Muslims to emigrate from Makkah to Abyssinia,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like 29:1–10, it directs believers unable to worship in their home land to migrate somewhere they can remain true to their religion.
rows.anchor: Similar to vv. 1–10, it indicates that those who are unable to worship God in the land in which they live should migrate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is related to 4:97, where angels question people who claim oppression whether God's earth was wide enough for them to migrate.
rows.anchor: In this regard, it is related to 4:97:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vestiges of divine mercy are rain and everything brought to life through it.
rows.anchor: The vestiges of God’s Mercy refers to the rain and all of the things that are given life through it (Bḍ).

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: The word translated vestiges, āthār, can also be read athar, meaning the effect of God's mercy.
rows.anchor: Vestiges translates āthār, which can also be read athar, meaning “the effect of God’s Mercy” (IJ, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recurring image of dead earth revived by God argues that He can resurrect decayed bones.
rows.anchor: this passage also uses such imagery to argue for God’s ability to resurrect decayed bones (Aj).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone can revive the earth and, being powerful over all things, can resurrect human beings.
rows.anchor: That is the Reviver of the dead thus indicates that God and no other has the ability to revive the earth,

rows.speaker: al-Tustarī
rows.claim: Al-Tustarī reads the verse outwardly as rain and inwardly as hearts brought to life through remembrance.
rows.anchor: In its outer meaning it refers to the rain, and in its inner meaning it alludes to the life of hearts through remembrance

rows.speaker: al-Ālūsī
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī argues that the verses' strong connection with what precedes makes a separate period unlikely.
rows.anchor: the strength of the connection of these verses to the preceding verses makes it seem unlikely that they are from a different period.

rows.speaker: author

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some called it Sūrat al-Maḍājiʿ, or Sūrah of the Beds, after believers who leave their beds to devote themselves to God.
rows.anchor: It was also known to some as Sūrat al-Maḍājiʿ, meaning “Sūrah of the Beds,”

rows.speaker: many
rows.claim: Many use its opening words to distinguish it from other sūrahs beginning with alif, lām, and mīm.
rows.anchor: Many also refer to this sūrah by its first words, “Alif, Lām, Mīm, the Revelation” (Al, Bq, Q),

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: Reports say the Prophet recited al-Mulk and al-Sajdah every night before sleeping, and al-Sajdah and al-Insān in Friday morning prayer.
rows.anchor: It is reported that the Prophet would read both al-Mulk

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some attribute the sūrah's special reverence to its concise treatment of the Quran's major themes.
rows.anchor: Some attribute the reverence for this sūrah to the way it covers the major themes of the Quran in a succinct manner.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first half treats revelation, God, creation especially of human beings, and Resurrection and Judgment.
rows.anchor: The first half of the sūrah discusses revelation (vv. 2–3), God (vv. 4–6), creation,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second half contrasts people who prostrate before God's signs with those who turn away, then presents Israel as guided while following God's signs.
rows.anchor: The second half provides an eloquent contrast between those who prostrate before God in beholding His signs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Children of Israel exemplify guidance so long as they follow God's signs.
rows.anchor: employing the Children of Israel as an example of those who were guided so long as they followed God’s signs (vv. 23–25).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion calls readers to reflect on past civilizations and God's signs in creation.
rows.anchor: A call to reflect upon the end of civilizations past and the signs of God in creation (vv. 26–27)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah closes by challenging the Prophet to confront the disbelievers and wait for the outcome.
rows.anchor: then segues into a call for the Prophet to challenge the disbelievers and await the answer (vv. 28–30).

none: Translation of the surah only; no commentary point.

rows.speaker: IJ, JJ
rows.claim: The question may mean: after our bodies decompose, are we to be reconstituted?
rows.anchor: The question in this verse may be seen as meaning, “When our bodies have decomposed, are we to be reconstituted?” (IJ, JJ).

rows.claim: The objection resembles the more common disbelief that people reduced to dust and bones will be resurrected.
rows.anchor: This is similar to the more common objection voiced by disbelievers,

rows.claim: For discussion of those who deny resurrection and meeting their Lord, the commentary directs readers to 30:8c and compares 6:31.
rows.anchor: Regarding those who deny resurrection and the meeting with their Lord (cf. 6:31), see 30:8c.

rows.claim: God shows mercy to believers who remember Him and perform the prayers commanded in the preceding verses; angels watch over them and pray for them.
rows.anchor: God has mercy upon the believers who remember God much and perform the prayers enjoined in the previous verses,

rows.anchor: which is understood to mean bringing them from being astray to being guided (Ṭ),

rows.claim: Sūrat Sabaʾ is Makkan.

rows.claim: The sūrah takes its name from the account of Sheba in verses 15–21.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the mention of the story of Sheba in vv. 15–21.

rows.anchor: Although some relate the story here to the queen of Sheba mentioned in 27:22–44,

rows.claim: Asked whether Sheba was a land or a woman, the Prophet reportedly answered that Sheba was a man with ten Arab sons, six auspicious to him and four inauspicious.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is reported to have replied, “Neither a land nor a woman, but a man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening praise and affirmation of omnipotence follow the previous sūrah's mention of the Trust, in its second-to-last verse.
rows.anchor: The beginning of this sūrah, with the mention of God’s Praise and Omnipotence,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This praise stresses God's complete independence of those who bear or neglect the Trust: bearing benefits them, neglect harms them, and their actions are not for God, whose praise is already complete.
rows.anchor: Such praise reiterates God’s complete independence of those who carry the Trust and those who neglect to carry it,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first two verses reaffirm God's nature, before the sūrah turns to the emptiness of disbelievers' claims.
rows.anchor: After the first two verses reaffirming the Nature of God, Sabaʾ launches into its primary subject, a critique of the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After its critique of disbelievers, the sūrah briefly recalls the accomplishments of David and Solomon.
rows.anchor: Brief allusions to the accomplishments of the prophets David (vv. 10–11) and Solomon (vv. 12–14)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of Sheba's arrogance over their good fortune leads to their destruction by a flood.
rows.anchor: whose arrogance at their good fortune led them to be destroyed by a flood (vv. 15–19).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two verses on Iblīs lead into challenges that the Prophet is instructed to put to the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: Two verses regarding the nature of Iblīs (vv. 20–21) then segue into a series of challenges the Prophet Muhammad is told to pose to the disbelievers (vv. 22–30).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afterlife account of leaders among disbelievers and their followers rejecting prophets leads into the next critique.
rows.anchor: An account of the discussion described as taking place sometime in the Hereafter between the leaders among the disbelievers and those who followed them in rejecting the prophets (vv. 31–33)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah critiques people whose wealth, power, and status mislead them into thinking they decide what is true.
rows.anchor: a critique of those whose wealth, power, and social status delude them into believing they are arbiters of truth (vv.34–45).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next section instructs the Prophet to clarify the nature of his mission.
rows.anchor: This is followed by injunctions to the Prophet Muhammad to clarify the nature of his mission (vv. 46–50),

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section addresses consequences for the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: which transitions into a concluding section on the consequences that will befall the disbelievers (vv. 51–54).
